subtitle: Step through 10 landmark turning points across 2,000 years—from Roman Bath curse tablets, Saxon wergild, and 1215 Magna Carta to Guy Fawkes, Elizabeth Fry, 1829 Bobbies, and 1984 Leicester DNA.

milestones.title: Roman Twelve Tables, Magistrates and Bath Curse Tablets
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did robbed bathers at Roman Bath scratch messages onto folded lead sheets?
milestones.imageCaption: Scratched Roman lead curse tablet (defixio) thrown into the Sacred Spring at Aquae Sulis (Bath).
milestones.catalyst: After AD 43, Rome introduced Britain’s first written laws judged by magistrates inside stone basilicas—yet victims had to catch thieves themselves or drop lead curse tablets into Bath’s spring.
milestones.turningPoint: Children visiting Roman market forums saw honest bronze scales and watched legionaries march past town gates.
milestones.impact: Established Britain’s earliest tradition of written court rules, though citizens received lighter fines than enslaved people.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 600–899): Ten-Person Tithings, the Hue and Cry, and Silver Wergild.

ks2.story: After AD 43, Rome introduced Britain’s first written laws judged by magistrates inside stone basilicas—yet victims had to catch thieves themselves or drop lead curse tablets into Bath’s spring.
ks2.significance: Established Britain’s earliest tradition of written court rules, though citizens received lighter fines than enslaved people.
ks2.childrenLife: Children visiting Roman market forums saw honest bronze scales and watched legionaries march past town gates.
ks2.quote: “To goddess Sulis Minerva: let whoever stole my warm cloak lose sleep until they carry it back to your temple!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did robbed bathers at Roman Bath scratch messages onto folded lead sheets?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Because Roman Britain had no police detectives, so victims begged goddess Sulis Minerva to punish unseen cloak thieves!

milestones.title: Ten-Person Tithings, the Hue and Cry, and Silver Wergild
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What deadly village problem did Anglo-Saxon silver "wergild" payments stop?
milestones.imageCaption: Struck ninth-century Anglo-Saxon silver penny used in royal coin and compensation systems.
milestones.provenance: Portable Antiquities Scheme / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)
milestones.catalyst: With zero police or prisons, every boy aged twelve joined a ten-person tithing, chased thieves on the Hue and Cry horn, and followed King Alfred’s written wergild compensation rules.
milestones.turningPoint: At age twelve, boys swore their tithing oath—promising nine neighbours to live honestly and sprint whenever the cow-horn blew!
milestones.impact: Proved close-knit rural villages could keep peace through neighbour responsibility and compensation.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 1079): William the Conqueror’s Norman Forest Laws and Poaching.

ks2.story: With zero police or prisons, every boy aged twelve joined a ten-person tithing, chased thieves on the Hue and Cry horn, and followed King Alfred’s written wergild compensation rules.
ks2.significance: Proved close-knit rural villages could keep peace through neighbour responsibility and compensation.
ks2.childrenLife: At age twelve, boys swore their tithing oath—promising nine neighbours to live honestly and sprint whenever the cow-horn blew!
ks2.quote: “Wer-gild meant person-price: silver coins healed village quarrels before swords were drawn!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What deadly village problem did Anglo-Saxon silver "wergild" payments stop?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Violent revenge "blood feuds" between angry families—settling injuries with agreed silver shillings instead!

milestones.title: William the Conqueror’s Norman Forest Laws and Poaching
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why do historians call hunting royal deer under Norman Forest Laws a "social crime"?
milestones.imageCaption: Wild fallow deer among oaks — protected for royal sport under harsh Norman Forest Laws.
milestones.catalyst: After 1066, William I kept Saxon tithings yet shifted court fines to his own treasury and fenced off vast woodlands like the New Forest, punishing peasant deer poaching severely.
milestones.turningPoint: Village children gathering fallen twigs had to watch carefully for royal foresters guarding the King’s deer.
milestones.impact: Turned crime into breaking the King’s Peace directly and inspired medieval Robin Hood outlaw ballads.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (1166 & 1215): Henry II’s Twelve-Person Juries, Magna Carta and Ending Ordeals.

ks2.story: After 1066, William I kept Saxon tithings yet shifted court fines to his own treasury and fenced off vast woodlands like the New Forest, punishing peasant deer poaching severely.
ks2.significance: Turned crime into breaking the King’s Peace directly and inspired medieval Robin Hood outlaw ballads.
ks2.childrenLife: Village children gathering fallen twigs had to watch carefully for royal foresters guarding the King’s deer.
ks2.quote: “Before 1066 woods fed the village; under Forest Law one royal stag mattered more than a hungry farmer!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why do historians call hunting royal deer under Norman Forest Laws a "social crime"?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Because ordinary villagers felt locking up woodlands was unfair and rarely informed on hungry neighbours!

milestones.title: Henry II’s Twelve-Person Juries, Magna Carta and Ending Ordeals
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which two events in 1215 cemented fair twelve-person jury trials in England?
milestones.imageCaption: Original 1215 sheepskin parchment of Magna Carta sealed beside the River Thames at Runnymede.
milestones.provenance: British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106 (Public Domain)
milestones.catalyst: King Henry II sent travelling judges across England to build one Common Law with twelve-person juries; in 1215 Magna Carta promised lawful trials and the Pope ended hot-iron ordeals.
milestones.turningPoint: Families saw royal assize judges ride into county towns while cathedral knockers still offered forty days of sanctuary.
milestones.impact: Created the enduring cornerstones of British justice: Common Law, twelve-person juries, and the rule of law.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (1567–1601): Tudor Vagrancy Whipping Laws and the 1601 Poor Law.

ks2.story: King Henry II sent travelling judges across England to build one Common Law with twelve-person juries; in 1215 Magna Carta promised lawful trials and the Pope ended hot-iron ordeals.
ks2.significance: Created the enduring cornerstones of British justice: Common Law, twelve-person juries, and the rule of law.
ks2.childrenLife: Families saw royal assize judges ride into county towns while cathedral knockers still offered forty days of sanctuary.
ks2.quote: “No free person shall be seized or imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of peers or the law of the land.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which two events in 1215 cemented fair twelve-person jury trials in England?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede AND Pope Innocent III banned priests from leading Trial by Ordeal!

milestones.title: Tudor Vagrancy Whipping Laws and the 1601 Poor Law
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Elizabeth I’s 1601 Poor Law treat sick locals differently from "sturdy beggars"?
milestones.imageCaption: Thomas Harman’s 1567 Elizabethan woodcut showing bound vagabonds whipped behind a horse-drawn cart.
milestones.catalyst: Rising prices and sheep pastures left thousands homeless; frightened Tudor towns whipped wandering "sturdy beggars" behind carts while helping elderly locals under the 1601 Poor Law.
milestones.turningPoint: Poor parish children were often apprenticed out to learn trades under the 1601 Elizabethan Poor Law.
milestones.impact: Showed how economic hardship and lack of police made early modern towns punish poverty harshly in public.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (5 Nov 1605): The Monteagle Letter, Guy Fawkes’s Lantern and 36 Barrels.

ks2.story: Rising prices and sheep pastures left thousands homeless; frightened Tudor towns whipped wandering "sturdy beggars" behind carts while helping elderly locals under the 1601 Poor Law.
ks2.significance: Showed how economic hardship and lack of police made early modern towns punish poverty harshly in public.
ks2.childrenLife: Poor parish children were often apprenticed out to learn trades under the 1601 Elizabethan Poor Law.
ks2.quote: “Towns without police feared every wandering stranger walking down the parish lane.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How did Elizabeth I’s 1601 Poor Law treat sick locals differently from "sturdy beggars"?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Elderly or sick locals received parish poor relief, whereas healthy "sturdy beggars" were whipped or sent to Bridewell workhouses!

milestones.title: The Monteagle Letter, Guy Fawkes’s Lantern and 36 Barrels
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What clue tipped off King James I to search the cellars beneath Parliament on 4–5 November 1605?
milestones.imageCaption: The real sheet-iron dark lantern held by Guy Fawkes beneath Parliament on 5 November 1605.
milestones.catalyst: Alerted by the Monteagle Letter, royal guards searched the Westminster undercroft before midnight and seized Guy Fawkes beside 36 barrels of gunpowder intended to blow up King and Parliament.
milestones.turningPoint: Every 5 November since 1605, London bells and bonfires marked the narrow escape of Parliament.
milestones.impact: Demonstrated why early modern monarchs treated religious and political High Treason with fierce public deterrence.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (1645–1736): East Anglian Witch Panics Ended by Scientific Proof.

ks2.story: Alerted by the Monteagle Letter, royal guards searched the Westminster undercroft before midnight and seized Guy Fawkes beside 36 barrels of gunpowder intended to blow up King and Parliament.
ks2.significance: Demonstrated why early modern monarchs treated religious and political High Treason with fierce public deterrence.
ks2.childrenLife: Every 5 November since 1605, London bells and bonfires marked the narrow escape of Parliament.
ks2.quote: “One sliding iron lantern shutter stood between thirty-six barrels of black powder and Westminster!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What clue tipped off King James I to search the cellars beneath Parliament on 4–5 November 1605?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: The anonymous Monteagle Letter warning a nobleman to avoid a "terrible blow" at the opening of Parliament!

milestones.title: East Anglian Witch Panics Ended by Scientific Proof
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did English witchcraft trials surge in 1645–1647 and disappear after 1660?
milestones.imageCaption: 1647 woodcut of Matthew Hopkins ("Witch Finder Generall") during the East Anglian Civil War witch panic.
milestones.catalyst: During 1645–1647 Civil War turmoil, Matthew Hopkins deprived isolated women of sleep to claim town fees—until post-1660 scientific thinking and calm judges ended witch trials by 1736.
milestones.turningPoint: Growing scientific discoveries taught young readers that germs and weather—not magic spells—caused storms and illness.
milestones.impact: Marked a decisive triumph of rational courtroom evidence and science over superstition.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (1787–1823): 220+ Bloody Code Laws, Australian Ships and Elizabeth Fry.

ks2.childrenLife: Growing scientific discoveries taught young readers that germs and weather—not magic spells—caused storms and illness.
ks2.quote: “Once judges banned sleepless bullying and demanded real proof, witchcraft trials vanished!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did English witchcraft trials surge in 1645–1647 and disappear after 1660?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Civil War chaos let Matthew Hopkins exploit fear for fees, until peace, the 1660 Royal Society, and strict judges demanded real proof!

milestones.title: 220+ Bloody Code Laws, Australian Ships and Elizabeth Fry
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Quaker reformer Elizabeth Fry prove inside Newgate Prison that "rehabilitation" worked?
milestones.imageCaption: Portrait engraving of Quaker prison reformer Elizabeth Fry (1780–1845), pioneer of humane prison schooling.
milestones.catalyst: When juries refused to hang petty thieves under the 220-crime Bloody Code, Britain shipped 160,000+ convicts to Australia (1787–1868) while Elizabeth Fry transformed Newgate (1813–1817).
milestones.turningPoint: Inside grim Newgate Prison in 1817, shivering children finally sat in Elizabeth Fry’s bright prison classroom!
milestones.impact: Proved harsh gallows terror had failed and inspired Robert Peel’s landmark 1823 Gaols Act.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 1829): Sir Robert Peel’s Unarmed London "Bobbies" at Scotland Yard.

ks2.story: When juries refused to hang petty thieves under the 220-crime Bloody Code, Britain shipped 160,000+ convicts to Australia (1787–1868) while Elizabeth Fry transformed Newgate (1813–1817).
ks2.significance: Proved harsh gallows terror had failed and inspired Robert Peel’s landmark 1823 Gaols Act.
ks2.childrenLife: Inside grim Newgate Prison in 1817, shivering children finally sat in Elizabeth Fry’s bright prison classroom!
ks2.quote: “Punishment is not for revenge, but to lessen crime and reform the prisoner.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How did Quaker reformer Elizabeth Fry prove inside Newgate Prison that "rehabilitation" worked?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: She brought clean clothes, female matrons, a school for prison children, and paid patchwork sewing skills!

milestones.title: Sir Robert Peel’s Unarmed London "Bobbies" at Scotland Yard
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Sir Robert Peel dress his 1829 London police in dark blue coats with wooden truncheons instead of army red and guns?
milestones.imageCaption: Painted 19th-century wooden police truncheons and alarm rattle carried by unarmed British constables.
milestones.provenance: Museum of Edinburgh / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
milestones.catalyst: Home Secretary Sir Robert Peel slashed over 180 Bloody Code hanging laws and launched 1,000 paid, blue-coated Metropolitan Police officers in 1829 to prevent crime on regular foot beats.
milestones.turningPoint: Victorian children lost in foggy London streets learned they could ask a top-hatted "Bobby" safely for help.
milestones.impact: Spread across every British county by 1856, replacing 1,800 years of unpaid neighbour chases with professional prevention.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (1901 & 1984): Scotland Yard Fingerprints (1901) and Leicester DNA Profiling (1984).

ks2.childrenLife: Victorian children lost in foggy London streets learned they could ask a top-hatted "Bobby" safely for help.
ks2.quote: “The police are the public and the public are the police.” — Sir Robert Peel’s Principles
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did Sir Robert Peel dress his 1829 London police in dark blue coats with wooden truncheons instead of army red and guns?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: To win citizens’ trust through peaceful "policing by consent" rather than ruling streets like soldiers!

milestones.title: Scotland Yard Fingerprints (1901) and Leicester DNA Profiling (1984)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What remarkable double victory did Sir Alec Jeffreys’s DNA test achieve in its very first murder inquiry?
milestones.imageCaption: Modern genetics micropipette and electrophoresis gel tank used in forensic DNA profiling.
milestones.catalyst: Following Scotland Yard’s 1901 Fingerprint Bureau, 1937 999 calls, and ending murder executions in 1965, Sir Alec Jeffreys discovered genetic DNA profiling at Leicester in September 1984.
milestones.turningPoint: School science pupils today learn about the same DNA double helix that solves cold cases and frees innocent people!
milestones.impact: Replaced ancient guesswork and superstition with microscopic scientific proof alongside modern cyber-crime policing.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Today: Fair twelve-person juries, unarmed policing by consent, and scientific forensics work side by side!

ks2.childrenLife: School science pupils today learn about the same DNA double helix that solves cold cases and frees innocent people!
ks2.quote: “At 9:05am in Leicester on 10 September 1984, a blurry X-ray film changed global justice forever!”

ks2.detectiveAnswer: It first proved an arrested teenager was completely INNOCENT, and then identified the true offender!
